claim: MYC oncogenes encode a family of related transcription factors that are overexpressed in a majority of cancers.
source: MYC oncogenes (c-, L-, and N-) encode a family of related transcription factors that are overexpressed in a majority of cancers and responsible for ~100,000 cancer-related deaths in the United States each year (Schaub et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schaub et al., 2018, which provides external evidence for this statement.

claim: MYC oncogenes are responsible for approximately 100,000 cancer-related deaths in the United States each year.
source: MYC oncogenes (c-, L-, and N-) encode a family of related transcription factors that are overexpressed in a majority of cancers and responsible for ~100,000 cancer-related deaths in the United States each year (Schaub et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schaub et al., 2018.

claim: MYC proteins dimerize with their obligate partner MAX to bind and regulate the expression of thousands of genes.
source: Capable of acting as both transcriptional activators and repressors, MYC proteins (hereafter 'MYC') dimerize with their obligate partner MAX (Blackwood and Eisenman, 1991) to bind and regulate the expression of thousands of genes connected to the cell cycle, protein synthesis, metabolism, genome stability, apoptosis, and angiogenesis (Tansey, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blackwood and Eisenman, 1991 and Tansey, 2014.

claim: MYC regulates genes connected to the cell cycle, protein synthesis, metabolism, genome stability, apoptosis, and angiogenesis.
source: Capable of acting as both transcriptional activators and repressors, MYC proteins (hereafter 'MYC') dimerize with their obligate partner MAX (Blackwood and Eisenman, 1991) to bind and regulate the expression of thousands of genes connected to the cell cycle, protein synthesis, metabolism, genome stability, apoptosis, and angiogenesis (Tansey, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tansey, 2014.

claim: Experimental inactivation of MYC promotes tumor regression in mice.
source: Fueled by reports that experimental inactivation of MYC promotes tumor regression in mice (Alimova et al., 2019; Beaulieu et al., 2019; Giuriato et al., 2006; Jain, 2002; Soucek et al., 2013), there is considerable interest in the idea that MYC inhibitors could form the basis of broadly effective anticancer therapies.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Alimova et al., 2019; Beaulieu et al., 2019; Giuriato et al., 2006; Jain, 2002; Soucek et al., 2013.

claim: MYC itself is widely viewed as undruggable.
source: MYC itself, however, is widely viewed as undruggable (Dang et al., 2017), meaning that effective strategies to pharmacologically inhibit MYC will most likely come from targeting the co-factors with which it interacts to drive and sustain the malignant state (Brockmann et al., 2013; Bryan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dang et al., 2017.

claim: Six evolutionarily conserved MYC boxes have been described.
source: In addition to the highly conserved basic helix-loop-helix domain that interacts with MAX, six evolutionarily conserved MYC boxes have been described (Baluapuri et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Baluapuri et al., 2020.

claim: MYC boxes are around 15 amino acid residues in length on average.
source: On average, MYC boxes are around 15 amino acid residues in length, and although it is clear that they each mediate multiple protein–protein interactions (Kalkat et al., 2018), a number of predominant interactors have been described for most of these segments
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kalkat et al., 2018.

claim: Mb0 interacts with the general transcription factor TFIIF to stimulate transcription.
source: Mb0, for example, interacts with the general transcription factor TFIIF to stimulate transcription (Kalkat et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kalkat et al., 2018.

claim: MbI interacts with the ubiquitin ligase SCFFBW7 to control MYC protein stability.
source: MbI interacts with the ubiquitin ligase SCFFBW7 to control MYC protein stability (Welcker et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Welcker et al., 2004.

claim: MbII interacts with the STAGA component TRRAP to regulate histone acetylation.
source: MbII interacts with the STAGA component TRRAP (McMahon et al., 1998) to regulate histone acetylation (Kalkat et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McMahon et al., 1998 and Kalkat et al., 2018.

claim: MbIIIb interacts with the chromatin-associated protein WDR5 to facilitate its recruitment to ribosomal protein genes.
source: MbIIIb interacts with the chromatin-associated protein WDR5 (Thomas et al., 2015) to facilitate its recruitment to ribosomal protein genes (Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thomas et al., 2015 and Thomas et al., 2019.

claim: MbIIIa is important for tumorigenesis.
source: The two remaining MYC boxes are less well understood, but MbIIIa is important for tumorigenesis (Herbst et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Herbst et al., 2005.

claim: MbIIIa is important for recruitment of HDAC3 to chromatin.
source: MbIIIa is important for tumorigenesis (Herbst et al., 2005) and recruitment of HDAC3 to chromatin (Kurland and Tansey, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kurland and Tansey, 2008.

claim: MbIV interacts with the ubiquitous chromatin-associated protein host cell factor (HCF)–1.
source: MbIV interacts with the ubiquitous chromatin-associated protein host cell factor (HCF)–1 (Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2016.

claim: HCF-1 is an essential nuclear protein.
source: HCF-1 is an essential nuclear protein (Goto et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goto et al., 1997.

claim: HCF-1 is synthesized as a 2035 amino acid precursor and proteolytically cleaved by O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT).
source: HCF-1 is an essential nuclear protein (Goto et al., 1997) that is synthesized as a 2035 amino acid precursor and proteolytically cleaved by O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) (Capotosti et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goto et al., 1997 and Capotosti et al., 2011.

claim: HCF-1 is cleaved into a collection of amino- (HCF-1N) and carboxy- (HCF-1C) terminal fragments that remain associated.
source: HCF-1 is an essential nuclear protein (Goto et al., 1997) that is synthesized as a 2035 amino acid precursor and proteolytically cleaved by O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) (Capotosti et al., 2011) into a collection of amino- (HCF-1N) and carboxy- (HCF-1C) terminal fragments that remain associated.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Capotosti et al., 2011.

claim: HCF-1 was first identified through its ability to assemble into a multiprotein–DNA complex with the herpes simplex virus transactivator VP16.
source: HCF-1 was first identified through its ability to assemble into a multiprotein–DNA complex with the herpes simplex virus transactivator VP16, but was later shown to function in uninfected cells as a co-factor for cellular transcription factors, and as part of the Sin3 and MLL/SET histone modifying complexes (Wysocka and Herr, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wysocka and Herr, 2003.

claim: HCF-1 functions in uninfected cells as a co-factor for cellular transcription factors.
source: HCF-1 was first identified through its ability to assemble into a multiprotein–DNA complex with the herpes simplex virus transactivator VP16, but was later shown to function in uninfected cells as a co-factor for cellular transcription factors, and as part of the Sin3 and MLL/SET histone modifying complexes (Wysocka and Herr, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wysocka and Herr, 2003.

claim: HCF-1 is part of the Sin3 and MLL/SET histone modifying complexes.
source: HCF-1 was first identified through its ability to assemble into a multiprotein–DNA complex with the herpes simplex virus transactivator VP16, but was later shown to function in uninfected cells as a co-factor for cellular transcription factors, and as part of the Sin3 and MLL/SET histone modifying complexes (Wysocka and Herr, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wysocka and Herr, 2003.

claim: The interaction of HCF-1 with VP16 is likely direct and is mediated by a tetrapeptide 'EHAY' motif in VP16 that binds to a region within the HCF-1N fragment known as the VP16-induced complex (VIC) domain.
source: The interaction of HCF-1 with VP16 is likely direct and is mediated by a tetrapeptide 'EHAY' motif in VP16 that binds to a region within the HCF-1N fragment known as the VP16-induced complex (VIC) domain (Freiman and Herr, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Freiman and Herr, 1997.

claim: The HCF-1-binding motif (HBM) has a consensus sequence of (D/E)-H-x-Y.
source: This four residue HCF-1-binding motif (HBM)—consensus (D/E)-H-x-Y—is present in other viral and cellular transcription factors that interact directly with the HCF-1 VIC domain, including key cell cycle regulators such as the E2F family of proteins (Tyagi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tyagi et al., 2007.

claim: The HBM is present in other viral and cellular transcription factors that interact directly with the HCF-1 VIC domain, including key cell cycle regulators such as the E2F family of proteins.
source: This four residue HCF-1-binding motif (HBM)—consensus (D/E)-H-x-Y—is present in other viral and cellular transcription factors that interact directly with the HCF-1 VIC domain, including key cell cycle regulators such as the E2F family of proteins (Tyagi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tyagi et al., 2007.

claim: HCF-1 was identified as a MYC-associated protein through proteomic approaches.
source: We identified HCF-1 as a MYC-associated protein through proteomic approaches, and demonstrated that the interaction occurs through the VIC domain of HCF-1 and an atypical HBM within MbIV that carries the sequence 'QHNY' (Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2016.

claim: The interaction between MYC and HCF-1 occurs through the VIC domain of HCF-1 and an atypical HBM within MbIV that carries the sequence 'QHNY'.
source: We identified HCF-1 as a MYC-associated protein through proteomic approaches, and demonstrated that the interaction occurs through the VIC domain of HCF-1 and an atypical HBM within MbIV that carries the sequence 'QHNY' (Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2016.

claim: Mutation of the four HBM residues to alanine disrupts the interaction of MYC with HCF-1 in vitro.
source: Mutation of these four HBM residues to alanine disrupts the interaction of MYC with HCF-1 in vitro and reduces the ability of MYC to promote murine fibroblast tumor growth in nude mice (Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2016.

claim: Mutation of the four HBM residues to alanine reduces the ability of MYC to promote murine fibroblast tumor growth in nude mice.
source: Mutation of these four HBM residues to alanine disrupts the interaction of MYC with HCF-1 in vitro and reduces the ability of MYC to promote murine fibroblast tumor growth in nude mice (Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2016.

claim: The 4A mutation disrupts the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
source: As expected, the 4A mutation disrupts the MYC–HCF-1 interaction, as do both histidine to glycine substitutions—confirming the essentiality of this core HBM residue to the MYC–HCF-1 association.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Histidine to glycine substitutions in the HBM disrupt the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
source: As expected, the 4A mutation disrupts the MYC–HCF-1 interaction, as do both histidine to glycine substitutions—confirming the essentiality of this core HBM residue to the MYC–HCF-1 association.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Replacing the MYC HBM with the canonical VP16 sequence increases the amount of HCF-1 recovered in the co-IP.
source: In contrast, replacing the MYC HBM with the canonical VP16 sequence increases the amount of HCF-1 recovered in the co-IP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The enhanced binding of the VP16 HBM MYC mutant to HCF-1 is also observed in vitro using purified recombinant MYC.
source: The enhanced binding of the VP16 HBM MYC mutant to HCF-1 is also observed in vitro using purified recombinant MYC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and in vitro translated HCF-1VIC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The enhanced binding of the VP16 HBM MYC mutant to HCF-1 is also observed in vitro using in vitro translated HCF-1VIC.
source: The enhanced binding of the VP16 HBM MYC mutant to HCF-1 is also observed in vitro using purified recombinant MYC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and in vitro translated HCF-1VIC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The MYC HBM is an authentic HBM.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that the MYC HBM is an authentic HBM, and that its variation from the canonical HBM sequence leads to a tempered interaction with HCF-1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The variation of the MYC HBM from the canonical HBM sequence leads to a tempered interaction with HCF-1.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that the MYC HBM is an authentic HBM, and that its variation from the canonical HBM sequence leads to a tempered interaction with HCF-1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: 4A switched cells have a selective advantage over the WT switch in their ability to grow without exogenous glutamine.
source: We see that 4A switched cells have a selective advantage over the WT switch in their ability to grow without exogenous glutamine (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The VP16 HBM mutant cells have a deficit in growth under glutamine-starvation conditions.
source: This advantage is likely due to loss of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction, as the VP16 HBM mutant cells have a corresponding deficit in growth under glutamine-starvation conditions (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cell cycle profiles for the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants are modestly altered compared to their WT counterparts.
source: When assayed in media replete with glutamine, cell cycle profiles for the two mutants are modestly altered compared to their WT counterparts, including small but statistically significant changes in the proportion of cells in G2/M (Figure 1G)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The proportion of cells in G2/M decreases for the 4A-expressing cells.
source: When assayed in media replete with glutamine, cell cycle profiles for the two mutants are modestly altered compared to their WT counterparts, including small but statistically significant changes in the proportion of cells in G2/M (Figure 1G), which again trend in opposite directions for the two MYC mutants—decreasing for the 4A-expressing cells and increasing for those that express the VP16 HBM mutant (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The proportion of cells in G2/M increases for those that express the VP16 HBM mutant.
source: When assayed in media replete with glutamine, cell cycle profiles for the two mutants are modestly altered compared to their WT counterparts, including small but statistically significant changes in the proportion of cells in G2/M (Figure 1G), which again trend in opposite directions for the two MYC mutants—decreasing for the 4A-expressing cells and increasing for those that express the VP16 HBM mutant (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 4A mutant cells are gradually lost from the culture over time in long-term growth assays in complete media.
source: Finally, in long-term growth assays in complete media, we observe that 4A mutant cells are gradually lost from the culture over time, whereas there is a significant enrichment of VP16 HBM cells, compared to the WT control (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of VP16 HBM cells in long-term growth assays in complete media, compared to the WT control.
source: Finally, in long-term growth assays in complete media, we observe that 4A mutant cells are gradually lost from the culture over time, whereas there is a significant enrichment of VP16 HBM cells, compared to the WT control (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The differences in representation of the two MYC mutants in these populations is unlikely due to apoptosis.
source: The differences in representation of the two MYC mutants in these populations is unlikely due to apoptosis—we observe no differences in the proportion of sub-G1 cells between the different switches (Figure 1G)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The differences in representation of the two MYC mutants track with changes in cell doubling time.
source: The differences in representation of the two MYC mutants in these populations is unlikely due to apoptosis—we observe no differences in the proportion of sub-G1 cells between the different switches (Figure 1G)—but tracks with changes in cell doubling time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D and Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Cell doubling time is increased for the 4A mutant cells.
source: The differences in representation of the two MYC mutants in these populations is unlikely due to apoptosis—we observe no differences in the proportion of sub-G1 cells between the different switches (Figure 1G)—but tracks with changes in cell doubling time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D and Figure 1—source data 1), which are increased for the 4A, and decreased for the VP16 HBM mutant cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Cell doubling time is decreased for the VP16 HBM mutant cells.
source: The differences in representation of the two MYC mutants in these populations is unlikely due to apoptosis—we observe no differences in the proportion of sub-G1 cells between the different switches (Figure 1G)—but tracks with changes in cell doubling time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D and Figure 1—source data 1), which are increased for the 4A, and decreased for the VP16 HBM mutant cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The MYC–HCF-1 interaction promotes the glutamine-dependency of BL cells in culture.
source: The altered and opposing impact of the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations in these assays leads us to conclude that the MYC–HCF-1 interaction promotes the glutamine-dependency—and rapid proliferative status—of these BL cells in culture.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figures 1F, 1G, 1H, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The MYC–HCF-1 interaction promotes the rapid proliferative status of BL cells in culture.
source: The altered and opposing impact of the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations in these assays leads us to conclude that the MYC–HCF-1 interaction promotes the glutamine-dependency—and rapid proliferative status—of these BL cells in culture.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figures 1F, 1G, 1H, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: More metabolites are significantly changed, and with a greater magnitude, for the 4A than the VP16 HBM MYC mutant.
source: In general, more metabolites are significantly changed, and with a greater magnitude, for the 4A than the VP16 HBM MYC mutant (Figure 2A–B and D–E and Figure 2—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–B and D–E and Figure 2—source data 1 and 2.

claim: For both 4A and VP16 HBM mutants, significantly changed metabolites group into a variety of categories, with a particular enrichment for those related to amino acid and lipids.
source: For both mutants, significantly changed metabolites group into a variety of categories, with a particular enrichment for those related to amino acid and lipids (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: A significant portion of the metabolite changes detected by both the RPLC and HILIC methods are in the same direction for the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants.
source: Comparing the direction of individual metabolite changes for the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), we note that a significant portion of the metabolite changes detected by both the RPLC and HILIC methods are in the same direction for the two MYC mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Shared metabolite changes between the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants fail to cluster strongly into biological pathways, with the only significant enrichment being glycerophospholipid metabolism.
source: In general, these shared metabolite changes fail to cluster strongly into biological pathways; the only significantly enrichment being glycerophospholipid metabolism (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Metabolite changes that occur in opposite directions for the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants show significant enrichment in pathways linked to nitrogen and amino acid metabolism.
source: Focusing on metabolite changes that occur in opposite directions for the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants, however, we observe significant enrichment in pathways linked to nitrogen and amino acid metabolism (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There is a clear anti-correlation between the impact of the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations on metabolites connected to aspartic acid.
source: There is a clear anti-correlation between the impact of the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations on metabolites connected to aspartic acid (Figure 2H)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Intracellular levels of glutamine (and associated metabolites) are increased in the 4A mutant cells.
source: we observe that intracellular levels of glutamine (and associated metabolites) are increased in the 4A and decreased in the VP16 HBM mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Intracellular levels of glutamine (and associated metabolites) are decreased in the VP16 HBM mutant cells.
source: we observe that intracellular levels of glutamine (and associated metabolites) are increased in the 4A and decreased in the VP16 HBM mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: There is a general tendency for amino acid levels to be increased in 4A mutant cells, compared to the WT switch.
source: Notably, these changes in intracellular amino acid levels are not confined to aspartic acid and glutamine, but there is a general tendency for amino acid levels to be increased in 4A and decreased in VP16 HBM mutant cells, compared to the WT switch (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Table 1.

claim: There is a general tendency for amino acid levels to be decreased in VP16 HBM mutant cells, compared to the WT switch.
source: Notably, these changes in intracellular amino acid levels are not confined to aspartic acid and glutamine, but there is a general tendency for amino acid levels to be increased in 4A and decreased in VP16 HBM mutant cells, compared to the WT switch (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Table 1.

claim: The MYC–HCF-1 interaction plays a global role in influencing intracellular amino acid levels in this setting.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that the MYC–HCF-1 interaction, directly or indirectly, plays a global role in influencing intracellular amino acid levels in this setting.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Table 1.

claim: Changes in the levels of ~4000 transcripts were observed in the 4A mutant cells compared to the WT switch.
source: Twenty-four hours after switching, we observed changes in the levels of ~4000 transcripts in the 4A, and ~3600 transcripts in the VP16 HBM, cells compared to the WT switch (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—source data 1 and 2.

claim: Changes in the levels of ~3600 transcripts were observed in the VP16 HBM mutant cells compared to the WT switch.
source: Twenty-four hours after switching, we observed changes in the levels of ~4000 transcripts in the 4A, and ~3600 transcripts in the VP16 HBM, cells compared to the WT switch (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—source data 1 and 2.

claim: Transcript changes are highly consistent among biological replicates.
source: These changes are highly consistent among biological replicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and modest in magnitude (Figure 3A), congruous with what is typically reported for MYC (Levens, 2002; Nie et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Transcript changes are modest in magnitude, congruous with what is typically reported for MYC.
source: These changes are highly consistent among biological replicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and modest in magnitude (Figure 3A), congruous with what is typically reported for MYC (Levens, 2002; Nie et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and citations to Levens, 2002 and Nie et al., 2012.

claim: Transcripts decreased by introduction of the 4A mutant are strongly linked to ribosome biogenesis, tRNA metabolism, and the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that transcripts decreased by introduction of the 4A mutant are strongly linked to ribosome biogenesis, tRNA metabolism, and the mitochondrial matrix (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Transcripts induced by the 4A mutant have links to transcription, cholesterol biosynthesis, and chromatin.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that transcripts decreased by introduction of the 4A mutant are strongly linked to ribosome biogenesis, tRNA metabolism, and the mitochondrial matrix (Figure 3B), while those that are induced have links to transcription, cholesterol biosynthesis, and chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For the VP16 HBM MYC mutant, decreased transcripts cluster in categories mostly related to the centrosome and the cell cycle.
source: For the VP16 HBM MYC mutant, decreased transcripts cluster in categories mostly related to the centrosome and the cell cycle (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Transcripts that are induced by the VP16 HBM protein have a pattern of clustering that is almost the exact opposite of those suppressed by the 4A mutant—including ribosome biogenesis, tRNA metabolism, and the mitochondrial matrix.
source: What is particularly striking, however, is that transcripts that are induced by the VP16 HBM protein have a pattern of clustering that is almost the exact opposite of those suppressed by the 4A mutant—including ribosome biogenesis, tRNA metabolism, and the mitochondrial matrix.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Transcripts reduced by the 4A mutant are strongly enriched in categories connected to ribosome biogenesis and the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Turning to transcripts that change in opposite directions with each mutant, those that are induced by the 4A mutant are moderately enriched in categories relating to kinase function and the cell cycle (Figure 3F, left), while those that are reduced by the 4A mutant are strongly enriched in categories connected to ribosome biogenesis and the mitochondrial matrix (Figure 3F, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The reciprocal changes observed for the GO categories in Figure 3B and C result from reciprocal changes in the expression of a common set of genes.
source: This analysis confirms that reciprocal changes we observed for the GO categories in Figure 3B and C results from reciprocal changes in the expression of a common set of genes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 3B, 3C, 3D, 3F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The MYC–HCF-1 interaction plays an important role in influencing the expression of genes that promote ribosome biogenesis and maintain mitochondrial function.
source: From our data, we conclude that the MYC–HCF-1 interaction plays an important role in influencing the expression of genes that promote ribosome biogenesis and maintain mitochondrial function.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The accumulation of amino acids observed with the 4A mutant is generally matched with a decrease in transcripts of cognate aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
source: Here we discovered that the accumulation of amino acids we observe with the 4A mutant is generally matched with a decrease in transcripts of cognate aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The decreased amino acid levels in the gain-of-function VP16 HBM mutant are matched with an increase in transcripts of cognate aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
source: Here we discovered that the accumulation of amino acids we observe with the 4A mutant is generally matched with a decrease in transcripts of cognate aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A)—and vice versa for the decreased amino acid levels in the gain-of-function VP16 HBM mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The reciprocal relationship of amino acid levels and tRNA ligase expression changes in response to the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants is consistent with the notion that defects in tRNA charging lead to compensatory changes in amino acid uptake.
source: The reciprocal relationship of amino acid levels and tRNA ligase expression changes in response to the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants is consistent with the notion that defects in tRNA charging lead to compensatory changes in amino acid uptake (Guan et al., 2014; Harding et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B, and is supported by citations to Guan et al., 2014 and Harding et al., 2000.

claim: A key biological context in which MYC and HCF-1 function together is protein synthesis.
source: The reciprocal relationship of amino acid levels and tRNA ligase expression changes in response to the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants is consistent with the notion that defects in tRNA charging lead to compensatory changes in amino acid uptake (Guan et al., 2014; Harding et al., 2000), further reinforcing the concept that a key biological context in which MYC and HCF-1 function together is protein synthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Addition of the dTAG-47 degrader results in the rapid and selective disappearance of the HCF-1N fragment.
source: Addition of the dTAG-47 degrader results in the rapid and selective disappearance of the HCF-1N fragment; the HCF-1C fragment is largely unaffected by up to 24 hr of dTAG-47 treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The HCF-1C fragment is largely unaffected by up to 24 hr of dTAG-47 treatment.
source: Addition of the dTAG-47 degrader results in the rapid and selective disappearance of the HCF-1N fragment; the HCF-1C fragment is largely unaffected by up to 24 hr of dTAG-47 treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Treated cells display altered cell cycle profiles.
source: Consistent with the known functions of HCF-1 (Julien and Herr, 2003), treated cells display altered cell cycle profiles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and a citation to Julien and Herr, 2003.

claim: Notable deficits in proliferation are only evident 48 hr after dTAG-47 addition.
source: but appear to be able to complete at least one round of cell division, as notable deficits in proliferation are only evident 48 hr after dTAG-47 addition (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: The HCF-1N fragment is essential in Ramos cells.
source: These data reveal that the HCF-1N fragment is essential in Ramos cells, and that early time point analyses should be resistant to complicating effects of HCF-1N degradation on cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Approximately 4500 significant transcript changes were identified associated with dTAG-47 treatment of sorted cells at 3 hr.
source: Despite the early time point, we identified ~4500 significant transcript changes associated with dTAG-47 treatment of sorted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—source data 2.

claim: Transcripts reduced by HCF-1N degradation are similar in kind to those reduced by the 4A mutation in MYC—including ribosome biogenesis and tRNA metabolic processes.
source: GO enrichment analysis showed that transcripts reduced by HCF-1N degradation are similar in kind to those reduced by the 4A mutation in MYC—including ribosome biogenesis and tRNA metabolic processes (Figure 4E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Transcripts induced by HCF-1N degradation tend to be cell cycle-connected.
source: while those induced by HCF-1N degradation tend to be cell cycle-connected (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Many of the genes that are differentially expressed upon HCF-1N degradation are also differentially expressed in the presence of either the 4A or VP16 HBM mutants.
source: Importantly, many of the genes that are differentially expressed upon HCF-1N degradation are also differentially expressed in the presence of either the 4A or VP16 HBM mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: A union set of ~450 genes—oppositely regulated by the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants—also change expression when HCF-1N is destroyed.
source: and we identified a union set of ~450 genes—oppositely regulated by the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants—the expression of which also changes when HCF-1N is destroyed (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Within the set of ~450 genes, loss of HCF-1N tends to mimic the loss of interaction 4A mutant.
source: Within this set, loss of HCF-1N tends to mimic the loss of interaction 4A mutant (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Within the cohort of transcripts that are reduced by both HCF-1N destruction and the 4A mutation, there is clear representation of genes connected to ribosome biogenesis and the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Moreover, within the cohort of transcripts that are reduced by both HCF-1N destruction and the 4A mutation, we see clear representation of genes connected to ribosome biogenesis and the mitochondrial matrix (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I and J.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis and mitochondrial matrix genes are directly controlled by the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
source: Although performing RNA-Seq at this early time likely underestimates the impact of loss of HCF-1N on the transcriptome, the presence of these ribosome biogenesis and mitochondrial matrix genes at the point of coalescence of all our RNA-Seq experiments strongly suggests that they are directly controlled by the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 4E, 4F, 4G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I and J.

claim: Approximately 1900 peaks for HCF-1N were identified in Ramos cells.
source: We performed ChIP-Seq using an antibody against the amino-terminus of HCF-1 (Machida et al., 2009), and identified ~1900 peaks for HCF-1N (Figure 5—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—source data 1 and a citation to Machida et al., 2009.

claim: The majority of HCF-1N peaks are promoter proximal.
source: We performed ChIP-Seq using an antibody against the amino-terminus of HCF-1 (Machida et al., 2009), and identified ~1900 peaks for HCF-1N (Figure 5—source data 1), the majority of which are promoter proximal (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HCF-1N peaks occur at genes enriched in functions connected to HCF-1, including the mitochondrial envelope, the cell cycle, as well as ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis.
source: These peaks occur at genes enriched in functions connected to HCF-1 (Minocha et al., 2019), including the mitochondrial envelope, the cell cycle, as well as ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and a citation to Minocha et al., 2019.

claim: HCF-1N peaks are enriched in DNA sequences linked to nuclear respiratory factor (NRF)–1, as well as the Sp1/Sp2 family of transcription factors.
source: Known (Figure 5C) and de novo (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) motif analysis revealed that HCF-1N peaks are enriched in DNA sequences linked to nuclear respiratory factor (NRF)–1, as well as the Sp1/Sp2 family of transcription factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The 'CATGCG' motif is a non-canonical E-box that MYC binds in vitro and in vivo.
source: Although linked to NRF-1, the 'CATGCG' motif is also a non-canonical E-box that MYC binds in vitro and in vivo (Blackwell et al., 1993; Haggerty et al., 2003; Morrish et al., 2003; Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blackwell et al., 1993; Haggerty et al., 2003; Morrish et al., 2003; Shi et al., 2014.

claim: 85% of HCF-1N peaks are also bound by MYC.
source: Overlaying these data with our previous ChIP-Seq analysis of MYC in Ramos cells (Thomas et al., 2019), we see that 85% of these HCF-1N peaks are also bound by MYC (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 2, and a citation to Thomas et al., 2019.

claim: The relationship between MYC and HCF-1N at co-binding sites is intimate.
source: The relationship between MYC and HCF-1N at these sites is intimate (Figure 5E and F and and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E, 5F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sites of co-binding tend to have higher signals for MYC than instances where MYC binds alone.
source: and sites of co-binding tend to have higher signals for MYC (Figure 5G) and HCF-1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) than instances where each protein binds alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Sites of co-binding tend to have higher signals for HCF-1 than instances where HCF-1 binds alone.
source: and sites of co-binding tend to have higher signals for MYC (Figure 5G) and HCF-1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) than instances where each protein binds alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Most HCF-1N binding sites on chromatin in Ramos cells occur at promoter proximal sites.
source: We conclude that most HCF-1N binding sites on chromatin in Ramos cells occur at promoter proximal sites and that the majority of these sites are also bound by MYC.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 5A, 5D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The majority of HCF-1N binding sites are also bound by MYC.
source: We conclude that most HCF-1N binding sites on chromatin in Ramos cells occur at promoter proximal sites and that the majority of these sites are also bound by MYC.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: There is little overlap of binding sites for MYC, WDR5, and HCF-1N in Ramos cells, with just ~5% of MYC–﻿HCF-1N co-bound sites also being bound by WDR5.
source: Interestingly, there is little overlap of binding sites for MYC, WDR5, and HCF-1N in Ramos cells, with just ~5% of MYC–﻿HCF-1N co-bound sites also being bound by WDR5 (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Of the 88 sites bound by all three proteins (MYC, WDR5, and HCF-1N), only three of these are sites where WDR5 has a functional role in MYC recruitment.
source: Moreover, of the 88 sites bound by all three proteins, only three of these are sites where WDR5 has a functional role in MYC recruitment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Approximately one-third of genes displaying promoter proximal binding of MYC and HCF-1N are differentially regulated in the presence of either the 4A or VP16 HBM MYC mutants.
source: Looking at genes displaying promoter proximal binding of MYC and HCF-1N—where clear gene assignments can be made—we see that approximately one-third of these genes are differentially regulated in the presence of either the 4A or VP16 HBM MYC mutants, and that this is significantly more than that predicted by chance alone (Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: For the 4A mutant, a slightly greater proportion of co-bound genes are downregulated.
source: For the 4A mutant, a slightly greater proportion of co-bound genes are downregulated, while the opposite is true for the VP16 HBM mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: For the VP16 HBM mutant, a slightly greater proportion of co-bound genes are upregulated.
source: For the 4A mutant, a slightly greater proportion of co-bound genes are downregulated, while the opposite is true for the VP16 HBM mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: A majority of MYC–HCF-1N co-bound genes that are oppositely impacted by the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants and deregulated by depletion of HCF-1N are connected to ribosome biogenesis and mitochondria.
source: A relatively small cohort of MYC–HCF-1N co-bound genes are oppositely impacted by the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G; '4A/VP'), but comparing these with those deregulated by depletion of HCF-1N (Figure 5J), we again see that a majority are connected to ribosome biogenesis and mitochondria
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Most MYC–HCF-1N co-bound genes that are oppositely impacted by the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants and deregulated by depletion of HCF-1N are positively regulated by HCF-1 and the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
source: A relatively small cohort of MYC–HCF-1N co-bound genes are oppositely impacted by the 4A and VP16 HBM mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G; '4A/VP'), but comparing these with those deregulated by depletion of HCF-1N (Figure 5J), we again see that a majority are connected to ribosome biogenesis and mitochondria, and that most are positively regulated by HCF-1 and the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis and mitochondrially connected genes are direct targets of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
source: Together, these data strongly support the notion that ribosome biogenesis and mitochondrially connected genes are direct targets of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Deletion of MbIV from N-MYC reduces the ability of MYC:MAX dimers to bind DNA.
source: It has been reported that deletion of MbIV from N-MYC reduces the ability of MYC:MAX dimers to bind DNA (Cowling et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cowling et al., 2006.

claim: Neither the 4A nor the VP16 HBM mutations have an overt impact on the binding of recombinant MYC:MAX dimers to DNA in vitro.
source: This phenotype is unrelated to the MYC HBM, however, as we determined that neither the 4A nor the VP16 HBM mutations have an overt impact on the binding of recombinant MYC:MAX dimers to DNA in vitro (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Binding of HCF-1N to chromatin is largely unaffected by the 4A or VP16 HBM mutations.
source: Binding of HCF-1N to chromatin is largely unaffected by the 4A or VP16 HBM mutations (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that MYC does not recruit HCF-1 to chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MYC does not recruit HCF-1 to chromatin.
source: Binding of HCF-1N to chromatin is largely unaffected by the 4A or VP16 HBM mutations (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that MYC does not recruit HCF-1 to chromatin.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Binding of MYC is subtly altered by both the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations.
source: Binding of MYC is subtly altered by both the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), but these changes are widespread and for the most part shared between the loss-of-function and gain-of-function MYC mutants (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Changes in MYC binding are widespread and for the most part shared between the loss-of-function and gain-of-function MYC mutants.
source: Binding of MYC is subtly altered by both the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), but these changes are widespread and for the most part shared between the loss-of-function and gain-of-function MYC mutants (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Focusing on the top 140 significant changes, the 4A and the VP16 HBM mutants both tend to have increased or expanded chromatin binding, compared to WT MYC.
source: Indeed, focusing on the top 140 significant changes, we see that the 4A and the VP16 HBM mutants both tend to have increased or expanded chromatin binding, compared to WT MYC (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The binding of MYC (and HCF-1) to chromatin is not impacted in opposite ways by the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations.
source: Visual inspection of the ChIP-Seq data (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) confirms the subtlety of these effects and reinforces the concept that the binding of MYC (and HCF-1) to chromatin is not impacted in opposite ways by the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Binding of MYC at genes flagged as direct targets is largely insensitive to the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations.
source: We further verified by ChIP-PCR—at genes flagged as direct targets in Figure 5 —that binding of MYC (Figure 6E) and HCF-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) is largely insensitive to the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Binding of HCF-1 at genes flagged as direct targets is largely insensitive to the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations.
source: We further verified by ChIP-PCR—at genes flagged as direct targets in Figure 5 —that binding of MYC (Figure 6E) and HCF-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) is largely insensitive to the 4A and VP16 HBM mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The HBM may play a modest role in chromatin targeting by MYC in cells, but this is likely to be independent of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
source: Thus, although the HBM may play a modest role in chromatin targeting by MYC in cells, this is likely to be independent of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 6A-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: MYC and HCF-1 interact to control the expression of ribosome biogenesis and mitochondrially connected genes through a co-recruitment-independent mechanism.
source: We conclude that MYC and HCF-1 interact to control the expression of ribosome biogenesis and mitochondrially connected genes through a co-recruitment-independent mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: 4A switched cells are significantly delayed in tumor growth compared to WT to WT switched cells.
source: As expected, the WT to WT switched cells develop tumors rapidly in vivo (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—source data 1), resulting in all mice reaching humane endpoints and being euthanized by 21 days post-injection (Figure 7C). In contrast, 4A-1, 4A-2, and ∆264 switched cells are significantly delayed, both in tumor growth (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—source data 1) and mortality (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: 4A-1, 4A-2, and ∆264 switched cells are significantly delayed in mortality compared to WT to WT switched cells.
source: As expected, the WT to WT switched cells develop tumors rapidly in vivo (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—source data 1), resulting in all mice reaching humane endpoints and being euthanized by 21 days post-injection (Figure 7C). In contrast, 4A-1, 4A-2, and ∆264 switched cells are significantly delayed, both in tumor growth (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 7—source data 1) and mortality (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Tumors from 4A-1, 4A-2, and ∆264 switched cells appear to originate from the outgrowth of unswitched cells in the injected populations.
source: Although 4A-1, 4A-2, and ∆264 switched cells did form tumors, these appear to originate from the outgrowth of unswitched cells in the injected populations, as ~75% of cells in these tumors are in their unswitched state (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The MYC–HCF-1 interaction is required for tumor growth.
source: In this assay, therefore, the MYC–HCF-1 interaction is required for tumor growth, and there is little if any difference between disruption of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction and disabling the majority of the nuclear functions of MYC.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 7B, 7C, and 7D.

claim: There is little if any difference between disruption of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction and disabling the majority of the nuclear functions of MYC in terms of tumor growth.
source: In this assay, therefore, the MYC–HCF-1 interaction is required for tumor growth, and there is little if any difference between disruption of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction and disabling the majority of the nuclear functions of MYC.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 7B, 7C, and 7D.

claim: For the 4A switches, tumors rapidly regressed after switching.
source: For the 4A switches, however, tumors rapidly regressed (Figure 7F), and all mice survived—and were tumor free—for the 60-day duration of the experiment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: All mice with 4A switches survived and were tumor free for the 60-day duration of the experiment.
source: For the 4A switches, however, tumors rapidly regressed (Figure 7F), and all mice survived—and were tumor free—for the 60-day duration of the experiment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: Regression of the 4A tumors occurs at a pace that is virtually indistinguishable from the ∆264 mutant.
source: Regression of the 4A tumors occurs at a pace that is virtually indistinguishable from the ∆264 mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: Regression of the 4A tumors is accompanied by high levels of apoptosis, as measured by Annexin V staining.
source: and like the ∆264 scenario, is accompanied by high levels of apoptosis, as measured by Annexin V staining (Figure 7H), caspase activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), and sub-G1 DNA content (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Regression of the 4A tumors is accompanied by high levels of apoptosis, as measured by caspase activity.
source: and like the ∆264 scenario, is accompanied by high levels of apoptosis, as measured by Annexin V staining (Figure 7H), caspase activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), and sub-G1 DNA content (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Regression of the 4A tumors is accompanied by high levels of apoptosis, as measured by sub-G1 DNA content.
source: and like the ∆264 scenario, is accompanied by high levels of apoptosis, as measured by Annexin V staining (Figure 7H), caspase activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), and sub-G1 DNA content (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The interaction of MYC with HCF-1 is essential for tumor maintenance in this context.
source: We conclude that the interaction of MYC with HCF-1 is essential for tumor maintenance in this context.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 7F, 7G, 7H, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, 1C, and 1D.

claim: Thousands of differentially expressed genes were identified in the mutant switch tumors.
source: Finally, we performed RNA-Seq on tumor material excised 48 hr after switching (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and Figure 7—source data 2). Thousands of differentially expressed genes were identified in the mutant switch tumors, many of which are shared between the 4A and ∆264 mutants—for both the decreased (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F) and induced (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G) directions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and Figure 7—source data 2.

claim: Many differentially expressed genes in the mutant switch tumors are shared between the 4A and ∆264 mutants—for both the decreased and induced directions.
source: Finally, we performed RNA-Seq on tumor material excised 48 hr after switching (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and Figure 7—source data 2). Thousands of differentially expressed genes were identified in the mutant switch tumors, many of which are shared between the 4A and ∆264 mutants—for both the decreased (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F) and induced (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G) directions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and 1G.

claim: Common reduced transcripts in the mutant switch tumors are enriched in those connected to ribosome biogenesis, translation, and mitochondrial envelope.
source: Common reduced transcripts are enriched in those connected to ribosome biogenesis, translation, and mitochondrial envelope (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Common induced transcripts in the mutant switch tumors are enriched for functions including transcription co-regulator activity, kinase binding, and the vacuole.
source: whereas those that are induced are enriched for functions including transcription co-regulator activity, kinase binding, and the vacuole (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

claim: More than 70% of the genes repressed in the 4A cell line are also repressed in either 4A-1 or 4A-2 tumors.
source: Indeed, more than 70% of the genes repressed in the 4A cell line are also repressed in either 4A-1 or 4A-2 tumors, and there is a common set of 942 genes that are shared between all three data sets (Figure 7I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: There is a common set of 942 genes that are repressed in the 4A cell line and both 4A-1 and 4A-2 tumors.
source: Indeed, more than 70% of the genes repressed in the 4A cell line are also repressed in either 4A-1 or 4A-2 tumors, and there is a common set of 942 genes that are shared between all three data sets (Figure 7I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The common set of 942 genes repressed in the 4A cell line and both 4A-1 and 4A-2 tumors coalesce on those connected to ribosome biogenesis, translation, and the mitochondria.
source: These genes coalesce on those connected to ribosome biogenesis, translation, and the mitochondria (Figure 7J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The overlap of induced genes between the 4A cell line and tumors was less pronounced (30%).
source: The overlap of induced genes was less pronounced (30%; Figure 7K) and these genes are less clustered, although we do observe modest enrichment in categories connected to metabolism, chromatin binding, and transcription coregulator activity (Figure 7L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Induced genes shared between the 4A cell line and tumors show modest enrichment in categories connected to metabolism, chromatin binding, and transcription coregulator activity.
source: The overlap of induced genes was less pronounced (30%; Figure 7K) and these genes are less clustered, although we do observe modest enrichment in categories connected to metabolism, chromatin binding, and transcription coregulator activity (Figure 7L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: A major function of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction is to stimulate ribosome production and mitochondrial vigor.
source: The recurring connections we observe between the MYC–HCF-1 interaction and ribosome biogenesis and mitochondrial function, both in vitro and in vivo, strongly support the notion that a major function of this interaction is to stimulate ribosome production and mitochondrial vigor, and that these actions are central for the ability of MYC to drive tumor onset and maintenance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3, 4, 5, and 7.

claim: The actions of the MYC–HCF-1 interaction to stimulate ribosome production and mitochondrial vigor are central for the ability of MYC to drive tumor onset and maintenance.
source: The recurring connections we observe between the MYC–HCF-1 interaction and ribosome biogenesis and mitochondrial function, both in vitro and in vivo, strongly support the notion that a major function of this interaction is to stimulate ribosome production and mitochondrial vigor, and that these actions are central for the ability of MYC to drive tumor onset and maintenance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3, 4, 5, and 7.
